The Dharma-discourse titled "Description of the Benefits of the Consecration of an Image of the Tathāgata," namely, the Avadāna of the Divine Meal.
[Modern Bangla scribble struck out: The Bhojanāvadāna [1v] || Homage be to the Buddha!

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows.

“Blessed One, what is the root of merit of sweeping and making offerings? What is the root of merit of offering a maṇḍala? What is the root of merit of taking refuge and receiving the precepts? What is the root of merit of the act of bowing to the Tathāgata with palms joined? Venerable Sir, what is the root of merit that is not exhausted by *saṃsāra*, does not diminish, and leads to inexhaustible *nirvāṇa*? What is the root of merit in fashioning an image of the Tathāgata? The Blessed One said:

There are five benefits in the act of sweeping and offering. What are the five? Namely: one’s own mind becomes serene; the deities become joyful; one performs and accumulates karma that leads to a beautiful appearance; and upon the dissolution of the body, one is reborn among the gods in the heavenly world of a Sugata. Ānanda, whoever with a serene mind makes a square mandala dedicated to the Tathāgata, for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Uttarakuru as the result of his sovereignty and lordship; and upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

[2r = 6r] We shall explain it. Let us now ask this very matter of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, the Dispeller of all doubts, the Teacher. Just as the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we retain it; and we shall explain it in detail and analyze it for the faithful brahmins and householders.
"Venerable sir, we ask the Blessed One about this very matter: Venerable sir, how many benefits are to be known for a person who commissions the making of an image of the Tathāgata?

"Excellent, excellent, monks! You have set out for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, in that you consider this very matter to be worthy of inquiry of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Therefore, monks, listen; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak."

"Monks, there are five benefits for a person who causes an image of the Tathāgata to be made. What are the five? One becomes possessed of a great celestial mansion, of great renown, immeasurable, of great power, of great energy, long-lived, famous, and full of happiness. Monks, this is the first benefit for a person who causes an image of the Tathāgata to be made."

Furthermore, monks, he becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; he has abundant wealth and resources, abundant internal property and assets, and a vast accumulation of money, grain, gold, treasuries, and storehouses; he possesses many elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and he has many friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations. Monks, this is the second benefit for a person who gives [an image] when a likeness of the Tathāgata is being made.

Furthermore, monks, he is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he is of a fair complexion, with a golden hue, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, and a broad forehead. His eyebrows and nose are well-proportioned, and he is endowed with all major and minor limbs, adorned with every kind of ornament. Monks, this is the third benefit for a person who gives when the Tathāgata’s image is being made.

Furthermore, monks, there is a universal monarch (cakravartin) who possesses a great retinue and is endowed with the seven jewels; he is surrounded by a thousand sons, and those who are his sons, wives, servants, or dependents—all of them serve him and attend to his every command. Monks, this is the fourth benefit for a person who gives [an image] when a likeness of the Tathāgata is being made.

Furthermore, monks, after the dissolution of the body, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods. Having been reborn there, he becomes incomparable and preeminent among other gods, sons of gods, and goddesses; as a king of gods, he shines forth by ten qualities: divine lifespan, divine complexion, divine strength, divine happiness, divine sovereignty and dominion, and divine [forms].
"O monks, this is to be known as the fifth benefit for a person who gives [an image] when the Tathāgata has a portrait made: [the enjoyment of] forms, sounds, smells, and tangibles."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Dharma discourse titled "The Description of the Benefits of Establishing an Image of the Tathāgata" is completed.
In the year 384, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, on Thursday.
